lessons.title: How tables relate one-to-many and many-to-many
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 1: How tables relate one-to-many and many-to-many

theory.contentHtml:
In the next lesson you will combine data from several tables. Before combining them, you need to know why the data was split apart in the first place - and where the links between tables come from.

Lesson contents:

  • 1. Why the data lives in more than one table
  • 2. Identifying columns and linking columns
  • 3. One-to-many
  • 4. Many-to-many and the bridge table
  • 5. The diagram and the join condition
  • 6. A table pointing at itself
  • Important Notes

1. Why the data lives in more than one table

Picture cramming everything into a single table - one row per order, with the customer's name, phone and city carried along:

+----------+------------+----------------+------------+--------+
| order_id | order_date |  customer_name |    phone   |  city  |
+----------+------------+----------------+------------+--------+
| 12       | 2024-02-03 | Benjamin Green | 0901234567 | Ha Noi |
| 45       | 2024-04-19 | Benjamin Green | 0901234567 | Ha Noi |
| 77       | 2024-06-02 | Benjamin Green | 0901234567 | Ha Noi |
+----------+------------+----------------+------------+--------+

Benjamin Green has 8 orders, so his phone number is copied 8 times. When he changes it, exactly 8 rows must be edited. Miss one and the database holds two different truths about the same person - and no query can tell which one is current.

The right move is to split them apart: customer information is written once in customers, while orders keeps only what belongs to an order, plus one column pointing back at the customer.

In a "relational database", a relation models a table. Tables can be connected by JOIN conditions; the term does not mean every table must have a relationship to another table.

The price you pay: to know whose order is whose, the two tables have to be put back together. That is exactly what JOIN does, and it is the next lesson.

2. Identifying columns and linking columns

The tables in this course use id to identify rows. In PostgreSQL, a PRIMARY KEY constraint enforces uniqueness and non-NULL values; it can contain one or several columns. A SQL table is not required to declare a primary key.

A table that points at another one often carries a column holding the other table's id. A declared FOREIGN KEY constraint checks that a linking value exists in the referenced table. Naming a column customer_id does not create that constraint. In this course they follow the naming convention <singular_table_name>_id:

+---------------+-------------------------+---------------------------+
|     Table     |      Linking column     |         Points at         |
+---------------+-------------------------+---------------------------+
| orders        | customer_id             | customers.id              |
| products      | category_id             | categories.id             |
| order_details | order_id, product_id    | orders.id, products.id    |
| reviews       | customer_id, product_id | customers.id, products.id |
+---------------+-------------------------+---------------------------+

Read the column name and you can guess the link. But this is a good naming convention, not a rule of SQL - in another database you will meet cust_no, fk_customer, or worse.

3. One-to-many

One customer can have many orders. One order belongs to exactly one customer. That is a one-to-many relationship - by far the most common kind.

You can see it without JOIN. Which orders belong to customer 28:

SELECT id, order_date, total_amount
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 28
LIMIT 10;

Eight rows come back, every one of them carrying customer_id = 28. Over in customers, the number 28 appears exactly once.

The reverse view says the same thing - each customer_id repeats as many times as that person has orders:

SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY order_count DESC
LIMIT 5;

The rule for spotting it: the linking column always sits on the "many" side. customer_id lives in orders; there is no order_id column in customers - this design stores one customer link on each order instead of putting a list of order IDs in one cell.

categories and products are one-to-many too: one category has many products, so category_id sits in products.

4. Many-to-many and the bridge table

Now the harder case. One order can hold many products. And one product also appears in many different orders. Both sides are "many" - a many-to-many relationship.

This shape leaves nowhere to put the linking column. Put product_id in orders and each order can buy exactly one product; put order_id in products and each product can be sold exactly once.

The answer is a third table in the middle - a bridge table - with one row per pair. Here it is order_details:

SELECT order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price
FROM order_details
WHERE order_id = 96
LIMIT 10;

Order 96 gives 4 rows: four different products inside one order.

Read the other direction, from the same table:

SELECT product_id, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS order_count
FROM order_details
WHERE product_id = 9
GROUP BY product_id
LIMIT 10;

Product 9 shows up in 18 orders. One table answering two opposite questions - that is what a bridge table does and a plain linking column usually cannot.

A bridge table often carries information that belongs to the pair, to neither side alone: quantity and unit_price are not attributes of the order, nor of the product, but of "this product in this order".

reviews is a bridge table as well, between customers and products, carrying rating and review_date.

5. The diagram and the join condition

The eight tables of this course link up like this - < points at the "many" side:

categories ──< products ──< order_details >── orders >── customers

customers ──< reviews >── products

employees          payments
(standalone)       (standalone)

order_details and reviews are the two bridge tables. employees and payments link to nothing at all - though employees will link back to itself in the Advanced course, see section 6.

In the next lesson, every join condition you write takes the same shape: the linking column on the "many" side equals the identifying column on the "one" side.

... ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
... ON order_details.product_id = products.id

Read the diagram and you can write the ON clause. That is the whole preparation for the JOIN lesson.

6. A table pointing at itself

One-to-many does not have to sit between two different tables. One employee has one manager; one manager has many employees. Both sides are rows of the same employees table.

This shape is solved with the very same tool - a linking column on the "many" side - except it points at the identifying column of that same table:

employees.manager_id  ──►  employees.id

The employees table in this course has no such column, which is why the diagram in section 5 leaves it standing alone. You will meet manager_id in the SQL Advanced course, walking the management tree with a recursive CTE.

Important Notes

  • One-to-many: the linking column sits on the "many" side - orders.customer_id, products.category_id.
  • Many-to-many: a bridge table is required - order_details, reviews. Information about the pair lives there.
  • A table pointing at itself is one-to-many too - employees.manager_id in the Advanced course.
  • Relationships in this sandbox are a design convention, not a constraint the engine enforces. No FOREIGN KEY is declared, so an order pointing at a customer who does not exist is accepted in silence:
INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount, status)
VALUES (9999, 12345, '2024-09-01', 1000000, 'Pending');

SELECT id, customer_id, status FROM orders WHERE id = 9999
LIMIT 10;

DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = 9999;

No customer carries id = 12345, yet no error is raised. A real database usually turns this constraint on to block exactly that case; here it is off, so keeping the data honest is the writer's job. The closing DELETE clears the row just inserted, so later lessons still count 101 orders.

lessons.title: Matching rows across tables with INNER JOIN
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 2: Matching rows across tables with INNER JOIN

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson contents:

  • 1. Why do we need JOIN?
  • 2. Basic INNER JOIN
  • 3. How to read JOIN results
  • Important Notes

1. Why do we need JOIN?

Data is split across multiple tables to avoid duplication. For example:

  • The orders table has customer_id - but not the customer's name
  • The customers table has full_name - but no order information

JOIN combines row pairs according to a join condition. Here it compares a linking column with an identifying column; the names need not match. ON matches only when the condition is TRUE, so NULL = NULL does not create a match.

2. Basic INNER JOIN

SELECT orders.id, customers.full_name, orders.total_amount
FROM orders
INNER JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
LIMIT 10;
  • FROM orders - the main table
  • INNER JOIN customers - the table to combine
  • ON orders.customer_id = customers.id - the join condition

INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables.

3. How to read JOIN results

Use table_name.column_name to avoid confusion when both tables have columns with the same name (e.g., both have id).

Table aliases let you write shorter queries:

SELECT o.id, c.full_name, o.total_amount
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
LIMIT 10;

Important Notes

  • INNER JOIN = keep only rows that match in both tables
  • Always specify table_name.column_name when columns share a name
  • Use table aliases to keep the code concise

After assigning orders o, reference that table as o.id, not orders.id, within the same query. Without ORDER BY, PostgreSQL does not guarantee row order, including for JOIN or LIMIT queries.

lessons.title: Keeping every left row with LEFT JOIN
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 3: Keeping every left row with LEFT JOIN

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson contents:

  • 1. What is LEFT JOIN?
  • 2. Comparing INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN
  • 3. Finding "missing" data with LEFT JOIN
  • Important Notes

1. What is LEFT JOIN?

SELECT c.full_name, o.id AS order_id, o.total_amount
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
LIMIT 10;

LEFT JOIN preserves every left-side row in the joined relation before WHERE/LIMIT. Multiple matching orders produce multiple rows for a customer; no match produces NULLs in the orders columns. This example has LIMIT 10, so the whole query returns at most 10 rows and need not display every customer.

2. Comparing INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN

+----------------------+------------+---------------------------------+
|                      | INNER JOIN |            LEFT JOIN            |
+----------------------+------------+---------------------------------+
| Has match            | ✅ Shown   | ✅ Shown                        |
| Left table no match  | ❌ Skipped | ✅ Shown (right columns = NULL) |
| Right table no match | ❌ Skipped | ❌ Skipped                      |
+----------------------+------------+---------------------------------+

3. Finding "missing" data with LEFT JOIN

Find customers who haven't bought anything:

SELECT c.full_name, c.email
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL
LIMIT 10;

This is a very common pattern: LEFT JOIN + WHERE ... IS NULL.

Important Notes

  • LEFT JOIN = keep the entire left table
  • To find "missing" rows, test a right-side column that cannot be NULL on a match. Here o.id IS NULL works because every sample order has an ID; an arbitrary nullable column such as email would be unsafe. NOT EXISTS also expresses the no-order condition.
  • PostgreSQL supports both RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN. Keeping the preserved table on the left with LEFT JOIN is often easier to read.

ON and WHERE are not equivalent with a LEFT JOIN

To preserve every left-side row while matching only completed orders, put the right-table filter in ON:

FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'Completed'

Moving o.status = 'Completed' to WHERE removes unmatched rows, whose o.status is NULL, and silently makes the join behave like an INNER JOIN. Put it in WHERE only when that removal is intentional.

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson contents:

  • Before joining: read the source data
  • 1. Joining 3+ tables
  • 2. JOIN + WHERE + GROUP BY
  • 3. The trap: JOIN multiplies rows
  • 4. Generate every combination with CROSS JOIN
  • Important Notes

Before joining: read the source data

Do not try to read the whole JOIN at once. First identify the table behind each alias and the columns used to connect it:

+-------+---------------+--------------------------------------------+
| Alias |     Table     |         Columns used in this lesson        |
+-------+---------------+--------------------------------------------+
| od    | order_details | order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price |
| o     | orders        | id, customer_id, status                    |
| c     | customers     | id, full_name                              |
| p     | products      | id, product_name, category_id              |
| cat   | categories    | id, category_name                          |
+-------+---------------+--------------------------------------------+

A small slice of the real sandbox data

The real tables contain more rows and columns. These are just the rows connected to order 1:

customers

+----+------------+
| id |  full_name |
+----+------------+
| 8  | Hugo Davis |
+----+------------+

orders

+----+-------------+-----------+
| id | customer_id |   status  |
+----+-------------+-----------+
| 1  | 8           | Completed |
+----+-------------+-----------+

order_details

+----+----------+------------+----------+------------+
| id | order_id | product_id | quantity | unit_price |
+----+----------+------------+----------+------------+
| 1  | 1        | 7          | 2        | 41990000   |
| 2  | 1        | 3          | 2        | 18990000   |
+----+----------+------------+----------+------------+

products

+----+--------------------+-------------+
| id |    product_name    | category_id |
+----+--------------------+-------------+
| 7  | Lenovo ThinkPad X1 | 2           |
| 3  | Xiaomi 14          | 1           |
+----+--------------------+-------------+

categories

+----+---------------+
| id | category_name |
+----+---------------+
| 2  | Laptop        |
| 1  | Phone         |
+----+---------------+

Follow each ON condition

Swapping the two sides of = does not change the match: od.order_id = o.id and o.id = od.order_id describe the same relationship. For readability, this lesson consistently writes foreign key on the left = primary key on the right:

  • od.order_id = o.id: which order the detail row belongs to.
  • o.customer_id = c.id: which customer owns the order.
  • od.product_id = p.id: which product the detail row describes.
  • p.category_id = cat.id: which category contains the product.

The connection map is:

customers.id  ←  orders.customer_id  ←  order_details.order_id
categories.id ←  products.category_id ← order_details.product_id

Starting from one order_details row, follow order_id to reach the order and customer; follow product_id to reach the product and category. Each JOIN below adds exactly one step along those two paths.

1. Joining 3+ tables

Get order details along with the product name and customer name:

SELECT c.full_name, p.product_name, od.quantity, od.unit_price
FROM order_details od
INNER JOIN orders o ON od.order_id = o.id
INNER JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
INNER JOIN products p ON od.product_id = p.id
LIMIT 10;

Each JOIN adds 1 table - you can JOIN as many tables as you need.

2. JOIN + WHERE + GROUP BY

Total revenue by product category:

SELECT cat.category_name,
       SUM(od.quantity * od.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM order_details od
INNER JOIN products p ON od.product_id = p.id
INNER JOIN categories cat ON p.category_id = cat.id
INNER JOIN orders o ON od.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status = 'Completed'
GROUP BY cat.category_name
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 10;

3. The trap: JOIN multiplies rows

Joining another table does not only add columns - it also adds rows. This is the quietest way a report goes wrong.

Total revenue, read straight from orders:

SELECT SUM(total_amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
LIMIT 10;

Now join the detail table, changing nothing else:

SELECT SUM(o.total_amount) AS revenue
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.id
LIMIT 10;

The number jumps from 4,503,000,000 to 12,019,000,000 - 2.67× larger. No error is raised, and the new figure still looks like a perfectly ordinary revenue number.

Look at a single order and it becomes obvious:

SELECT o.id, o.total_amount, od.product_id, od.quantity
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.id = 96
LIMIT 10;

Order 96 has 4 products, so after the join it becomes 4 rows - and total_amount of 62,000,000 sits intact on every one of them. SUM adds it four times. This is the one-to-many relationship showing itself: join toward the "many" side and each row on the "one" side is duplicated exactly as many times as it has matches.

How to fix it. The rule: add up a number in the table it belongs to.

  • total_amount belongs to the order → sum it in orders, without joining the details.
  • Revenue per line item belongs to order_details → sum quantity * unit_price right there.

For COUNT, DISTINCT is the rescue:

SELECT COUNT(o.id) AS wrong, COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) AS correct
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN order_details od ON od.order_id = o.id
LIMIT 10;

260 and 101. The right answer is 101 - exactly the number of orders that have line items.

One note about this dataset: SUM(total_amount) (4.503 billion) and SUM(quantity * unit_price) (8.041 billion) do not match, because total_amount is a stored total generated independently of the detail lines. A stored total drifting away from its details is very common in the wild. What matters here is picking the right level to add up, not that those two figures should agree.

4. Generate every combination with CROSS JOIN

Suppose a shop offers 3 shirt colors and 4 sizes. To build all 12 color-size variants, you need to pair every color with every size. This is what CROSS JOIN is for.

CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product of two tables: each row on the left is paired with every row on the right. Its syntax has no ON condition:

SELECT c.full_name, cat.category_name
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN categories cat
ORDER BY c.id, cat.id
LIMIT 10;

The course sandbox has 30 customers and 5 categories, so the join produces 30 × 5 = 150 rows. The full Cartesian product has 150 pairs, but the query with LIMIT 10 returns at most 10 rows. PostgreSQL can stop early without physically producing all 150 pairs. You can check the total directly:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS combination_count
FROM customers
CROSS JOIN categories
LIMIT 10;

If the left table has m rows and the right table has n rows, the result has m × n rows. If either table is empty, the result is empty too.

When should you use it?

  • Generate every color × size variant.
  • Build a store × date grid to find dates with no transactions.
  • Run every scenario × parameter set stored in a configuration table.

Watch the row count

CROSS JOIN can grow a result very quickly. For example, 10,000 products × 365 dates produces 3,650,000 rows before any filtering or aggregation. Estimate the row count before running it on large tables.

A missing join condition can also create a Cartesian-product result by accident. The query below is wrong if the goal is to connect each order to its actual customer:

-- Wrong if the goal is to connect each order to its actual customer
SELECT c.full_name, o.id
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN orders o
LIMIT 10;

When two tables have a relationship, use INNER JOIN ... ON ... with the appropriate key condition. Use CROSS JOIN only when you genuinely want every possible pair.

Important Notes

  • Joining multiple tables: follow the foreign key chain
  • You can combine INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN in the same query
  • When joining multiple tables, use consistent aliases to keep the query short and easy to trace
  • Joining toward the "many" side multiplies rows - re-check every SUM/COUNT after adding a table
  • CROSS JOIN creates every combination between two tables - estimate left rows × right rows before running it

questions.prompt: Which rows does INNER JOIN return?

options.label: B
options.text: Only rows that match in both tables

options.label: C
options.text: All rows from the left table

options.label: D
options.text: All rows from the right table

questions.explanation: INNER JOIN returns only rows with matching values in both tables. Non-matching rows are dropped.

questions.prompt: With non-NULL order IDs o.id, which JOIN pattern finds customers who have not placed an order?

options.label: B
options.text: LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL

options.label: C
options.text: WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)

options.label: D
options.text: LEFT JOIN ... WHERE left_table.column IS NULL

questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN supplies NULL order columns when there is no matching order. Since real order IDs are non-NULL, WHERE o.id IS NULL keeps customers without orders. Correlated NOT EXISTS is also correct; the EXISTS alternative instead finds customers with orders.

questions.prompt: In FROM orders JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id, how do you select the order ID unambiguously?
questions.explanation: When two tables have a same-named column, you must specify table_name.column_name to avoid ambiguity (ambiguous column error).

questions.prompt: Which statement about RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN in PostgreSQL is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: PostgreSQL supports RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN; LEFT JOIN is often clearer when preserving the left table

options.label: B
options.text: RIGHT JOIN always means INNER JOIN

options.label: C
options.text: RIGHT JOIN works only without ON

options.label: D
options.text: PostgreSQL does not support FULL OUTER JOIN

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL supports RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN. LEFT JOIN is often easier to read because the preserved table stays on the left; choose the direction that expresses the business meaning.

questions.prompt: One product appears in many orders, and one order contains many products. Which design is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Add a product_id column to orders

options.label: B
options.text: Add an order_id column to products

options.label: C
options.text: Use a bridge table order_details, one row per order–product pair

options.label: D
options.text: Use LEFT JOIN instead of INNER JOIN

questions.explanation: A many-to-many relationship leaves nowhere to put the linking column - add product_id to orders and each order can buy exactly one product. The answer is a bridge table, and it can also carry information about the pair such as quantity and unit_price.

questions.prompt: SUM(o.total_amount) after joining orders with order_details returns a figure larger than reality. Why?

options.label: B
options.text: Each order is duplicated once per detail line, so total_amount is added several times

options.label: C
options.text: total_amount is stored incorrectly in the orders table

options.label: D
options.text: GROUP BY is missing, so SUM misbehaves

questions.explanation: Joining toward the "many" side duplicates each row on the "one" side exactly as many times as it has matches. Order 96 has 4 detail lines, so its total_amount is added 4 times. The fix: add up a number in the table it belongs to, or use COUNT(DISTINCT ...) when counting.

practice.title: Practice: Joining orders with customers
practice.summaryHtml: Join orders with customer information to get a consolidated view of completed orders.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.html:
• Returned columns: id (order id), full_name (customer name), city (customer's city), total_amount (order value), status (order status)
  • Match each order with the customer who placed it; keep only orders with status = 'Completed'
  • Sort by order id ascending

sections.title: Schema
sections.html:
Table: customers

+-----------+---------+-------------------------------+
|   Column  |   Type  |          Description          |
+-----------+---------+-------------------------------+
| id        | INTEGER | Customer ID                   |
| full_name | TEXT    | Customer full name            |
| city      | TEXT    | City where the customer lives |
+-----------+---------+-------------------------------+

Each row contains information about one customer.

Table: orders

+--------------+----------------+-----------------------------------------+
|    Column    |      Type      |               Description               |
+--------------+----------------+-----------------------------------------+
| id           | INTEGER        | Order ID                                |
| customer_id  | INTEGER        | ID of the customer who placed the order |
| total_amount | NUMERIC(18, 2) | Total order amount (VND)                |
| status       | TEXT           | Order processing status                 |
+--------------+----------------+-----------------------------------------+

Each row contains information about one order.

sections.title: Sample data
sections.html:
Table: customers

+----+-----------+--------+
| id | full_name |  city  |
+----+-----------+--------+
| 1  | Chloe     | Hanoi  |
| 2  | Daniel    | TP.HCM |
| 3  | Carl      | Denver |
+----+-----------+--------+

Table: orders

+----+-------------+--------------+-----------+
| id | customer_id | total_amount |   status  |
+----+-------------+--------------+-----------+
| 1  | 2           | 5000000      | Completed |
| 2  | 1           | 8000000      | Completed |
| 3  | 1           | 3000000      | Shipping  |
| 4  | 3           | 12000000     | Cancelled |
+----+-------------+--------------+-----------+

sections.title: Expected output
sections.html:
+----+-----------+--------+--------------+-----------+
| id | full_name |  city  | total_amount |   status  |
+----+-----------+--------+--------------+-----------+
| 1  | Daniel    | TP.HCM | 5000000.00   | Completed |
| 2  | Chloe     | Hanoi  | 8000000.00   | Completed |
+----+-----------+--------+--------------+-----------+

practice.title: Practice: Products by category
practice.summaryHtml: Retrieve the list of products with their category name, sorted by category then price descending.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.html:
• Returned columns:
    • category_name: the product's category name
    • product_name: the product name
    • price: the product price
  • Only include products that have a valid category (match each product with its corresponding category)
  • Sort by category_name ascending, then by price descending

sections.title: Schema
sections.html:
Table: categories

+---------------+---------+-----------------------+
|     Column    |   Type  |      Description      |
+---------------+---------+-----------------------+
| id            | INTEGER | Category ID           |
| category_name | TEXT    | Product category name |
+---------------+---------+-----------------------+

Each row contains information about one product category.

Table: products

+--------------+----------------+------------------------------+
|    Column    |      Type      |          Description         |
+--------------+----------------+------------------------------+
| id           | INTEGER        | Product ID                   |
| product_name | TEXT           | Product name                 |
| price        | NUMERIC(18, 2) | Selling price (VND)          |
| category_id  | INTEGER        | ID of the product's category |
+--------------+----------------+------------------------------+

Each row contains information about one product.

+----+---------------+
| id | category_name |
+----+---------------+
| 1  | Laptop        |
| 2  | Accessory     |

| id |  product_name  |   price  | category_id |

| 1  | MacBook Pro    | 45000000 | 1           |
| 2  | Dell XPS       | 35000000 | 1           |

  • List only customers who have never had any order

  • Edge case: the result may be empty if every customer has purchased

sections.title: Schema

Table: customers

+-----------+---------+-------------------------------+
|   Column  |   Type  |          Description          |
+-----------+---------+-------------------------------+
| id        | INTEGER | Customer ID                   |

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson contents:

  • 1. What is a subquery?
  • 2. Two independent classifications
  • 3. Non-correlated subqueries
  • 4. Correlated subqueries
  • 5. IN, EXISTS, and NULL
  • Important notes

1. What is a subquery?

A subquery is a SELECT statement placed inside another SQL statement. The outer query can use its result as a value, a set, or an existence check.

Read a query in terms of the data relationship it describes. The database optimizer may rewrite the execution plan, so do not assume that a subquery always runs first or exactly once.

2. Two independent classifications

Subqueries are commonly described along two different axes:

+---------------------------------+----------------+---------------------------------------------------+
|            Criterion            |      Type      |                      Meaning                      |
+---------------------------------+----------------+---------------------------------------------------+
| Relationship to the outer query | Non-correlated | Does not reference a column from the outer query  |
| Relationship to the outer query | Correlated     | References a column or alias from the outer query |
| Result shape                    | Scalar         | Is used where one value is required               |
| Result shape                    | Set            | Supplies rows to a test such as IN or EXISTS      |
+---------------------------------+----------------+---------------------------------------------------+

These axes do not replace each other. A scalar subquery can be either correlated or non-correlated.

3. Non-correlated subqueries

Find employees whose salary is above the company-wide average:

SELECT full_name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)
LIMIT 10;

The subquery does not reference the current row of the outer query. AVG() produces one average value, so the result can appear on the right side of >.

In PostgreSQL, a scalar subquery must return one column and at most one row: zero rows produce NULL; more than one row raises an error instead of choosing the first row. AVG() without GROUP BY/HAVING returns one row even for empty input; its value is then NULL, and salary > NULL keeps no employee.

4. Correlated subqueries

Find employees whose salary is above the average for their own department:

SELECT e.full_name, e.department, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (
    SELECT AVG(e2.salary)
    FROM employees e2
    WHERE e2.department = e.department
)
LIMIT 10;

e.department belongs to the outer query. Because the subquery depends on the department of the current e row, this is a correlated subquery. Logically, the condition is evaluated for each outer row; the optimizer still decides the physical execution strategy.

5. IN, EXISTS, and NULL

IN expresses whether a value belongs to the result set:

SELECT DISTINCT c.full_name
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
INNER JOIN order_details od ON o.id = od.order_id
WHERE od.product_id IN (
    SELECT id FROM products WHERE category_id = 2
)
LIMIT 10;

EXISTS fits a question about whether a matching row exists. Do not choose between IN and EXISTS only from subquery size; choose by meaning and measure the execution plan on representative data.

For negation, take care with NOT IN: if the result set contains NULL, the condition can become UNKNOWN. The next lesson covers EXISTS, NOT EXISTS, and this case in more detail.

Important notes

  • Scalar describes a value position; correlated describes a reference to the outer query.
  • An aggregate such as AVG() without GROUP BY or HAVING guarantees one result row and fits a scalar comparison.
  • IN checks membership in a set; EXISTS checks whether a row exists.
  • The subqueries in these examples are enclosed in parentheses ().

SELECT DISTINCT over names returns distinct names. For a list of individual customers, keep c.id with c.full_name or use EXISTS so customers who share a name are not merged.

lessons.title: Conditional branching with CASE WHEN
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 10: Conditional branching with CASE WHEN

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson contents:

  • 1. Basic CASE WHEN
  • 2. CASE WHEN in SELECT
  • 3. CASE WHEN + GROUP BY
  • Important Notes

1. Basic CASE WHEN

Like IF-ELSE in programming:

CASE
    WHEN condition_1 THEN result_1
    WHEN condition_2 THEN result_2
    ELSE default_result
END

2. CASE WHEN in SELECT

Classify salary:

SELECT full_name, salary,
    CASE
        WHEN salary IS NULL THEN 'Unknown'
        WHEN salary >= 30000000 THEN 'High'
        WHEN salary >= 20000000 THEN 'Medium'
        ELSE 'Low'
    END AS salary_level
FROM employees
LIMIT 10;

3. CASE WHEN + GROUP BY

Count employees by salary level:

SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN salary IS NULL THEN 'Unknown'
        WHEN salary >= 30000000 THEN 'High'
        WHEN salary >= 20000000 THEN 'Medium'
        ELSE 'Low'
    END AS salary_level,
    COUNT(*) AS num_emp
FROM employees
GROUP BY salary_level
LIMIT 10;

Important Notes

  • Always include END to close the CASE
  • ELSE is optional - if omitted, it defaults to NULL
  • CASE WHEN is checked in order - it stops at the first condition that is true

For NULL salaries, threshold comparisons yield UNKNOWN; the salary IS NULL branch avoids labeling an unknown salary Low. PostgreSQL requires THEN/ELSE results to resolve to one compatible type: keep these labels consistently TEXT rather than mixing a number with a label such as ELSE 'Low'. CASE selects the first TRUE branch, but does not prevent every planning-time error, such as a constant 1/0 expression.

Lesson contents:

  • 1. String functions
  • 2. Date and time functions
  • 3. COALESCE - replacing NULL
  • Important notes

1. String functions

+------------------------------------+----------------+-----------------------------------------+
|              Function              |   Description  |                 Example                 |
+------------------------------------+----------------+-----------------------------------------+
| UPPER(s) / LOWER(s)                | Change case    | UPPER('abc') → 'ABC'                    |
| LENGTH(s)                          | String length  | LENGTH('Hello') → 5                     |
| substring(s FROM start FOR length) | Slice a string | substring('Hello' FROM 1 FOR 3) → 'Hel' |
| `                                  | NULL           | orCONCAT(...)`                          |
+------------------------------------+----------------+-----------------------------------------+

PostgreSQL supports both substr and substring; substring(... FROM ... FOR ...) is the explicit PostgreSQL form. || returns NULL when either operand is NULL, while CONCAT skips NULL arguments.

LEFT, substr and substring take TEXT, not a direct DATE argument. For example, LEFT(DATE '2024-06-15', 7) reports an argument type error even though PostgreSQL has LEFT. Use to_char(order_date, 'YYYY-MM') to display a month; cast to order_date::text only when you actually need string processing.

2. Date and time functions

order_date is a DATE, not a string. Keep a typed DATE value while calculating:

EXTRACT(YEAR FROM order_date)::int       -- 2024
EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date)::int      -- 6
date_trunc('month', order_date)::date    -- 2024-06-01
to_char(date_trunc('month', order_date)::date, 'YYYY-MM') -- display label

Use date_trunc when grouping by month; use to_char only in the outer SELECT when a YYYY-MM label is needed.

3. COALESCE - replacing NULL

SELECT full_name,
       COALESCE(email, 'No email') AS email
FROM employees
LIMIT 10;

COALESCE(a, b) returns a when a is not NULL; otherwise it returns b.

Important notes

  • Use || when NULL should propagate; use CONCAT when you want to concatenate non-NULL parts.
  • Use NULLIF(denominator, 0) before division when a denominator may be zero.
  • COALESCE(a, b, c) returns the first non-NULL value.

COALESCE replaces NULL, not the empty string ''. Its arguments need compatible types: COALESCE(salary, 0) returns a number; use COALESCE(salary::text, 'Unknown') for a text label. LENGTH(TEXT) counts characters rather than bytes; OCTET_LENGTH counts bytes. PostgreSQL integer division gives 5 / 2 = 2; use 5::numeric / 2 for a fractional result. A zero denominator raises an error; NULLIF(denominator, 0) changes it to NULL so division returns NULL.

lessons.title: Checking existence with EXISTS and NOT EXISTS
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 12: Checking existence with EXISTS and NOT EXISTS

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson contents:

  • 1. What is EXISTS?
  • 2. NOT EXISTS and missing data
  • 3. Choosing EXISTS or IN
  • 4. The NULL trap with NOT IN
  • Important notes

1. What is EXISTS?

EXISTS is true when its subquery returns at least one row. The selected value does not matter, so SELECT 1 is a common convention:

SELECT c.full_name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM orders o
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
)
LIMIT 10;

The subquery references c.id from the outer query, so it is correlated. The query returns customers who have placed an order.

2. NOT EXISTS and missing data

SELECT p.product_name
FROM products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM reviews r
    WHERE r.product_id = p.id
)
LIMIT 10;

NOT EXISTS keeps products with no matching review row. The same requirement can sometimes be expressed with a LEFT JOIN followed by a NULL check on the right-side key.

3. Choosing EXISTS or IN

+------------------------------------------------+--------------------+
|                     Purpose                    | Natural expression |
+------------------------------------------------+--------------------+
| Check whether a value belongs to a result set  | IN                 |
| Check whether at least one matching row exists | EXISTS             |
| Check whether no matching row exists           | NOT EXISTS         |
+------------------------------------------------+--------------------+

There is no universal rule that EXISTS is faster than IN. The optimizer, indexes, row counts, and value distribution determine the execution plan. When performance matters, use EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and benchmark representative data.

4. The NULL trap with NOT IN

If a NOT IN subquery returns any NULL, the comparison can become UNKNOWN and keep no rows. When the inner column may contain NULL, NOT EXISTS with an explicit matching condition is usually safer.

Important notes

  • EXISTS cares only whether the subquery has a row, not about the value in its SELECT list.
  • A correlated subquery references a column or alias from the outer query.
  • Choose syntax by meaning first, then measure performance on real data.

EXPLAIN displays the planned execution; ANALYZE executes the query to measure it. Use it with the SELECT being investigated. For x NOT IN (1, NULL), x=1 yields FALSE and x=2 yields UNKNOWN; WHERE keeps neither. EXISTS depends on rows, not NULL values: EXISTS (SELECT NULL) is TRUE because one row exists.

headings.text: 4. The NULL trap with NOT IN

questions.prompt: What is the most direct way to compare a column with a scalar subquery guaranteed to return one value?

options.label: A
options.text: Use a comparison operator such as =, >, or <

options.label: D
options.text: A scalar subquery cannot be compared

questions.explanation: A scalar subquery can occupy a value position, for example salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) ...). IN is still valid for a one-element set, so it is not forbidden; a comparison operator is simply the direct expression when the subquery is guaranteed to be scalar.

questions.prompt: What does COALESCE(email, 'N/A') return when email IS NULL?
questions.explanation: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument. When email IS NULL, COALESCE(email, 'N/A') = 'N/A'. It is commonly used to display a default value when a column can be NULL.

questions.prompt: In what order does CASE WHEN evaluate conditions?

options.label: B
options.text: Top to bottom, stopping at the first condition that is true

options.label: C
options.text: Checks all, picks the last result

questions.explanation: CASE WHEN evaluates conditions from TOP TO BOTTOM. When it hits the FIRST WHEN that matches TRUE, it returns that result and stops - later WHENs are skipped. Put the most specific condition FIRST.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which form concatenates strings while propagating NULL?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL supports both || and CONCAT. a || b returns NULL when either side is NULL, while CONCAT skips NULL arguments. Choose the behavior that matches the data meaning.

questions.prompt: What is NOT EXISTS used for?

options.label: B
options.text: Find rows for which the subquery returns NO result

options.label: D
options.text: Check whether a column is NULL

questions.explanation: NOT EXISTS is used to find rows that have no matching row in the subquery. A typical pattern: find customers who have never placed an order = WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id).

questions.prompt: Which query contains a correlated subquery?

options.label: A
options.text: A subquery with e2.department = e.department, where e belongs to the outer query

options.label: B
options.text: SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees, with no outer-query reference

options.label: C
options.text: SELECT id FROM products WHERE category_id = 2, with no outer-query reference

options.label: D
options.text: An independent SELECT 1 that reads no column

questions.explanation: A correlated subquery references a column or alias from the outer query. In e2.department = e.department, alias e belongs to the outer query; the other choices do not need the current outer row.

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson contents:

  • 1. JOIN + CASE WHEN + GROUP BY
  • 2. Subquery + JOIN
  • 3. Data analysis pattern
  • Important Notes

1. JOIN + CASE WHEN + GROUP BY

Classify customers by total spending:

SELECT c.full_name,
       SUM(o.total_amount) AS total_spent,
       CASE
           WHEN SUM(o.total_amount) >= 50000000 THEN 'VIP'
           WHEN SUM(o.total_amount) >= 20000000 THEN 'Loyal'
           ELSE 'Regular'
       END AS customer_tier
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'Completed'
GROUP BY c.id, c.full_name
ORDER BY total_spent DESC
LIMIT 10;

2. Subquery + JOIN

Top 3 best-selling products:

SELECT p.product_name, sub.total_sold
FROM (
    SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) AS total_sold
    FROM order_details
    GROUP BY product_id
    HAVING SUM(quantity) IS NOT NULL
    ORDER BY total_sold DESC, product_id
    LIMIT 3
) sub
INNER JOIN products p ON sub.product_id = p.id
ORDER BY sub.total_sold DESC, p.id
LIMIT 10;

A subquery in FROM → is called a Derived Table.

3. Data analysis pattern

When building a report, always follow the flow:

  1. Identify the data source (which tables?)
  2. JOIN the related tables
  3. WHERE to filter the needed data
  4. GROUP BY to group along the analysis dimension
  5. HAVING to filter groups (if needed)
  6. ORDER BY to sort the result

Important Notes

  • Give a derived table an alias (e.g., sub) to reference its columns clearly; PostgreSQL 16 and later allow an omitted alias in FROM
  • For complex queries, build step by step - test each part as you go

Group by the identifier together with the display name so distinct entities with the same name remain separate. Names are not declared UNIQUE; grouping by names alone can incorrectly merge their data.

The inner ORDER BY selects the three products; the outermost ORDER BY guarantees their display order after JOIN. product_id makes the selection stable when totals tie. The reporting steps describe a logical model, not a required physical execution order.

The Top 3 considers known sales totals only; HAVING excludes all-NULL quantity groups before ORDER BY DESC.

questions.prompt: What is a subquery in FROM called?
questions.explanation: A subquery in FROM is a derived table, providing rows and columns within the current query. It does not create a TEMP TABLE or a materialized view in the database.

questions.prompt: When you write SUM(o.total_amount) inside a CASE WHEN within a SELECT that has GROUP BY, over what scope does SUM compute?
questions.explanation: When SUM sits inside a CASE WHEN within a SELECT that has GROUP BY, SUM computes over EACH GROUP BY GROUP (not the whole table). The CASE WHEN is an expression evaluated for each group after grouping.

questions.prompt: Why should you give a derived table an alias?

options.label: A
options.text: To reference the subquery and columns clearly

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL 16 and later allow a subquery in FROM without an alias. Still, FROM (SELECT ...) AS sub is easier to read and lets a JOIN reference sub.column_name clearly. An alias does not sort, filter NULL or limit results.

    • Otherwise → 'Regular'
  • Collapse the result to one row per customer
  • Sort: by total_spent descending
  • Edge case: a customer with no Completed order does not appear in the result

practice.title: Practice: Revenue dashboard
practice.summaryHtml: Build a revenue report by product category, counting only completed orders.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.html:
• Columns to return: category_name, products_sold, total_revenue, avg_revenue
  • Combine information from order line items, products, categories, and orders to have all the data the report needs
  • Only count line items belonging to orders with status = 'Completed'
  • products_sold: the total quantity of products sold in the category
  • total_revenue: the category's total revenue (each line item contributes its quantity times its unit price)
  • avg_revenue: the average revenue per order line item in the category - keep the raw value, do not round
  • One row per category, sorted by total revenue descending

| quantity   | INTEGER        | Quantity ordered                     |
| unit_price | NUMERIC(18, 2) | Unit price at purchase time (VND)    |

Each row contains one line item in an order.

practice.title: Practice: Final recap exercise
practice.summaryHtml: Build a product review report including category, average score, and number of reviews.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.html:
• Columns to return: product_name, category_name, avg_score, num_reviews
  • Only consider products with at least 2 reviews
  • avg_score: the product's average review rating
  • num_reviews: the number of reviews for the product
